mainEntity.name: How much does a Peugeot 2008 1.4 or 1.6 HDi engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rebuilt Peugeot 2008 HDi engine typically costs £1,800-£3,100 supply-only, depending on engine size and condition. The 1.4 HDi (8HZ) is cheaper to replace - from £1,800 - while the 1.6 HDi (9HZ) ranges £2,900-£3,100. Used engines start from £520. Supply & fit adds £400-£800 labour.

mainEntity.name: What are the most common Peugeot 2008 1.6 HDi engine problems?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common Peugeot 2008 1.6 HDi (9HZ) engine problems are EGR valve failure causing rough idle and power loss, DPF blockage from short-journey driving triggering anti-pollution faults, and turbo actuator failure causing loss of boost. Fuel injector issues and oil dilution from injector seal leaks are also reported.

mainEntity.name: What causes the Peugeot 2008 1.4 HDi anti-pollution fault?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 'anti-pollution fault' warning on a Peugeot 2008 1.4 HDi is usually caused by DPF blockage from short-journey driving preventing regeneration, or EGR valve carbon buildup. The 1.4 HDi's DPF is sensitive to urban driving patterns, and the warning often appears alongside loss of power or limp mode.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine on a Peugeot 2008 1.4 or 1.6 HDi?

acceptedAnswer.text: Replacing a Peugeot 2008 1.4 or 1.6 HDi engine is worthwhile if the vehicle is otherwise sound and the replacement cost stays below the vehicle's value. With 2008 HDi values typically £3,000-£9,000, a rebuilt engine at £1,800-£3,100 represents a significant but often justifiable investment. For sub-£4,000 examples, a used engine from £520 may be more economical.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Peugeot 2008 1.6 HDi engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With proper maintenance, the Peugeot 2008 1.6 HDi (9HZ) engine typically reaches 150,000-200,000 miles. The 1.4 HDi (8HZ) is similarly durable but suffers from DPF sensitivity in urban use. Regular oil changes, EGR cleaning and DPF-friendly driving (regular motorway runs) are essential for longevity.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between Peugeot 2008 HDi and BlueHDi engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peugeot 2008 HDi engines (8HZ, 9HZ) are pre-Euro 6 units fitted to first-generation 2008s from 2013-2016. They have simpler emissions hardware (EGR + DPF) but no AdBlue system. BlueHDi engines (DV6C, DV5RC) replaced them from 2015 onwards with Euro 6 compliance, adding AdBlue/SCR systems for lower NOx emissions but greater complexity. HDi engines are generally simpler and cheaper to maintain.

historyTimeline.h2: Peugeot 2008 1.4 & 1.6 HDi - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The Peugeot 2008 1.4 and 1.6 HDi diesel engines powered the first-generation (A94) 2008 from launch in 2013 until the arrival of the BlueHDi range in 2015. The 1.4 HDi (8HZ / DV4TD) was the entry-level diesel, offering modest 68hp output and excellent economy for budget-conscious buyers. The 1.6 HDi (9HZ / DV6TED4) was the higher-output workhorse, delivering 92hp and stronger torque for motorway driving. Both engines are pre-Euro 6, meaning they lack the complex AdBlue systems of later BlueHDi units - simpler emissions hardware, but with their own EGR and DPF challenges.

milestones.description: **2013** - Peugeot 2008 launched with 1.4 HDi 68hp (8HZ) and 1.6 HDi 92hp (9HZ) diesel options
**2014** - 1.6 HDi carries over with minor ECU updates for emissions compliance
**2015** - BlueHDi 1.6L (DV6C) introduced, replacing both HDi units in most trims
**2016** - Final year for 1.4 HDi and 1.6 HDi in UK 2008 models

historyTimeline.closingNote: Every 8HZ and 9HZ engine fitted to the Peugeot 2008 1.4 and 1.6 HDi is covered below, with UK rebuilt pricing and known failure points.

commonProblems.h2: Peugeot 2008 1.4 & 1.6 HDi Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The Peugeot 2008 1.4 and 1.6 HDi engines are generally robust workhorses, but age, mileage and the demands of diesel emissions systems create distinct failure patterns. The 1.6 HDi's EGR valve, DPF and turbo actuator are the most common failure points, while the 1.4 HDi suffers from turbo wastegate and glow plug issues. Unlike later BlueHDi units, these pre-Euro 6 engines lack AdBlue complexity - but DPF and EGR problems remain significant drivers of replacement enquiries. Every rebuilt Peugeot 2008 HDi engine through EnginesMarket includes upgraded components addressing the original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: EGR Valve Failure - Why Peugeot 2008 1.6 HDi Engines Lose Power and Run Roughly
problems.rootCause: Carbon buildup from exhaust gases sticks the EGR valve open or closed, disrupting the air-fuel mixture and triggering fault codes. Owners report intermittent power loss, rough idle and engine management lights. The issue is often accompanied by black smoke from the exhaust.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove valve, clean with solvent, reinstall and reset ECU
repairOptions.longevity: Works if valve mechanism isn't worn or seized

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply and fit new EGR valve, gaskets, recalibrate system
repairOptions.longevity: Restores function; may need intake manifold clean too

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit rebuilt 1.6 HDi with new EGR, turbo check, 12-month warranty
repairOptions.longevity: Needed if stuck EGR caused turbo or piston damage

problems.recommendation: EGR issues on the 2008 1.6 HDi are common but usually fixable without engine replacement. Clean or replace the valve early to avoid secondary damage - a £200 specialist clean can prevent a £2,900 engine replacement. Only consider a rebuilt engine if the fault has already caused turbo or internal wear.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt 9HZ Peugeot 2008 1.6 HDi engine prices

problems.h4: DPF Blockage - Why Peugeot 2008 HDi Engines Trigger Anti-Pollution Faults
problems.rootCause: Short-journey driving prevents the DPF from reaching regeneration temperature, causing soot buildup that eventually blocks exhaust flow. Owners report "anti-pollution fault" warnings, limp mode and loss of power. The 1.4 HDi is particularly susceptible to DPF-related warning lights.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Diagnostic reset, extended high-speed drive or forced regen cycle
repairOptions.longevity: Works if blockage is early-stage and sensors are functional

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove DPF for off-car cleaning or supply fitted replacement unit
repairOptions.longevity: Restores function if substrate isn't melted or cracked

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit rebuilt HDi with new DPF, EGR, 12-month warranty
repairOptions.longevity: Needed if blockage caused turbo or piston damage

problems.recommendation: For a Peugeot 2008 HDi used mainly for short trips, invest in periodic DPF cleaning before blockage becomes severe. The 1.4 HDi's DPF warnings are often the first sign of trouble - address them promptly. If the DPF has caused turbo damage or excessive backpressure, a rebuilt engine with fresh emissions components offers better long-term value.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt HDi engine prices for your Peugeot 2008 diesel

problems.h4: Turbocharger Failure - Why Peugeot 2008 HDi Engines Lose Boost and Smoke Excessively
problems.rootCause: The turbocharger's wastegate actuator can stick, or the variable geometry mechanism can seize from carbon buildup. Owners report loss of power, black smoke under load and unusual turbo noises. The 1.4 HDi's turbo wastegate is a known weak point, while the 1.6 HDi's turbo actuator can fail at higher mileages.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of actuator or complete turbo unit with new oil feed lines
repairOptions.longevity: Restores boost; viable if no engine damage

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete rebuilt unit with new turbo assembly and revised oil feeds
repairOptions.longevity: Required if turbo failure has caused engine damage

problems.recommendation: If your Peugeot 2008 HDi has lost power and is smoking excessively, have the turbo system inspected immediately. Actuator replacement is often sufficient if caught early. Once turbo debris has contaminated the oil system or caused bearing damage, a full rebuilt engine is the safest option.
